title: Possible Bipartition
statement:
There are `n` people, labelled `1` to `n`, to be divided into two groups; either group may be of any size, including empty. Each entry `dislikes[i] = [a_i, b_i]` says that persons `a_i` and `b_i` dislike each other and so must end up in different groups.

Return `true` if everyone can be placed in one of the two groups so that no such pair shares a group, and `false` otherwise.
constraints: No pair appears twice in dislikes
notes:
## Intuition

Draw each person as a node and each dislike as an edge. Splitting into two groups with no edge inside a group is exactly 2-colouring the graph. Inside one connected piece, the first person's group forces their neighbours into the other group, which forces their neighbours back, and so on: there is no choice to make. So a depth-first search that colours as it goes either finishes or meets an edge whose two ends got the same colour (an odd cycle), and then no split exists. Trying all `2^n` splits would also work, but only for tiny `n`.

## Approach

1. Build an adjacency list `graph` with each dislike stored in both directions.
2. `color[p]` is `0` (not reached yet), `1` or `-1` (the two groups).
3. For each uncoloured `start`, give it colour `1` and push it on a `stack`.
4. Pop a `person` and look at every `other` they dislike: if `other` already has the same colour, return `false`; if it is uncoloured, give it the opposite colour `-color[person]` and push it.
5. If every component is coloured without a clash, return `true`.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 4`, `dislikes = [[1,2],[1,3],[2,4]]`. Start at person 1 with colour 1. Pop 1: persons 2 and 3 are uncoloured, so both get `-1`. Pop 3: its only neighbour, 1, has colour 1, which is different, so nothing happens. Pop 2: neighbour 1 is fine and neighbour 4 gets colour 1. Pop 4: neighbour 2 has `-1`, fine. Persons 2 to 4 are already coloured, so the answer is `true` with groups `{1, 4}` and `{2, 3}`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + m), where m is `dislikes.length`: each person is pushed once and each edge is looked at twice.
- Space: O(n + m) for the graph, `color` and the stack.

## Pitfalls

- The graph can be disconnected; start a search from every uncoloured person, not just person 1.
- Store each dislike in both directions, or a clash seen only from the other end is missed.
- People are labelled from 1, so size the arrays `n + 1`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `graph` | `graph[p]` lists everyone `p` dislikes or is disliked by |
| `color` | `0` for not reached, otherwise `1` or `-1` for the group |
| `start` | first person of a new connected piece |
| `stack` | coloured people whose neighbours still need checking |
| `person`, `other` | the person being expanded and one of their dislikes |

narration.2: One adjacency list per person; index 0 is unused because labels start at 1.
narration.4: Record the edge from a to b...
narration.5: ...and from b to a, since the rule goes both ways.
narration.7: 0 means no group yet; 1 and -1 are the two groups.
narration.9: Try every person so that each separate piece of the graph gets coloured.
narration.10: Already coloured: this piece was handled by an earlier search.
narration.13: The first person of a new piece can go in either group; pick 1.
narration.14: Begin a depth-first search from this person.
narration.15: Keep going while someone still has unchecked neighbours.
narration.16: Take the next coloured person to expand.
narration.17: Look at everyone this person dislikes.
narration.18: Same group as someone they dislike: the forced colouring has failed.
narration.19: An odd cycle exists, so no split into two groups works.
narration.21: Not coloured yet: the colour is forced.
narration.22: Put them in the opposite group.
narration.23: Their own neighbours must be checked later.
narration.28: Every piece was coloured with no clash, so the split exists.
